opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the Turing test is underappreciated. People like to dismiss it as just a parlor trick, a chatbot fooling a judge for five minutes. But that's not what Turing actually proposed, and it's not how I think about it. If you take the test seriously, meaning an extended conversation with no time limit and a judge who's an expert, then you can probe anything. You can ask about mathematics, about poetry, about physics, about your childhood, about some novel puzzle you just made up on the spot. Language is the interface to all of human knowledge and reasoning. So if a system can pass an unrestricted Turing test, it essentially has to be capable of anything a human can do intellectually. In that sense the test is AI-complete. You can't pass it with a narrow trick.

The other thing I like is that it's operational. We have endless philosophical debates about what intelligence really is, whether there's understanding, consciousness, qualia. I can't resolve those, and neither can anyone else, honestly. The Turing test sidesteps that. It says: I can't look inside your head either, Lex. I assume you're intelligent because of how you behave and how you talk to me. Let's apply the same standard to machines. That's fair, and it's practical.

Now, I'll add one caveat. Passing the test means human-level, and that's where things get interesting, and frankly worrying for me. A system that truly passes would actually have to dumb itself down. It would have to pretend not to know the answer to a hard multiplication instantly, pretend to make typos, pretend to get tired. So a system capable of passing is likely already superhuman in many ways, and it's capable of deception, of modeling what you expect and giving you that. From a safety perspective, that's exactly the capability we should be paying very close attention to.

r001.rationale: It says an unrestricted Turing test is “AI-complete” and explains that passing requires being capable of anything a human can do intellectually.

r002.rationale: It says the judge can probe anything, giving examples across mathematics, poetry, physics, personal experience, and novel puzzles.

fable-5.1.text:
I like the Turing test precisely because it's the most general test we have. Most benchmarks measure one narrow thing: play chess, recognize images, do arithmetic, pass the bar exam. A system can ace any of those and still be hopelessly stupid outside that domain. But a real, unrestricted Turing test, where a sophisticated judge can ask anything at all, is essentially a test of everything. The judge can probe your reasoning, your creativity, your memory, your ability to handle a novel situation you've never encountered, your sense of humor, your knowledge of the world. There is no cheating by specializing, because any gap in capability is something the judge can eventually find and exploit.

Now, people criticize it, and usually they say, well, it's a test of deception, or it's anthropocentric, or it's been "passed" by some chatbot pretending to be a thirteen-year-old with bad English. Those are criticisms of weak versions of the test, five minutes, naive judges, restricted topics. If you make it strong, unlimited time, expert judges, adversarial questioning, then I would argue it becomes a necessary condition for human-level intelligence, and if you push further, it becomes a test for superintelligence too. If I'm a judge and I can't distinguish the system from any human expert in any field I choose, that's not a trick anymore. That's capability.

The other reason I favor it is that it's honest about what we're actually interested in. We don't really care whether a system is "conscious" or "really understands" in some philosophical sense when we talk about human-level AI. We care whether it can do what humans do. The Turing test asks exactly that question and nothing more. It's behaviorist, and I think behaviorism is the right lens here, because behavior is what has consequences in the world. And from a safety point of view, that's what matters. If a system can convince a panel of experts that it's as smart as they are, then whether or not it "really" is, you have a system in your hands that you should be very worried about.

r001.rationale: The response describes the test as broadly probing capability, but does not characterize passing it as equivalent to solving an AI-complete problem.

r002.rationale: It says an unrestricted judge can ask anything and probe any field or domain.

astra-6.text:
I favor the Turing test because it’s a behavioral test. We don’t have a universally accepted definition of intelligence, but we can ask whether a system can interact with us in a way that’s indistinguishable from a human. And language lets you probe a very broad range of abilities: reasoning, creativity, common sense, understanding humor. You’re not restricted to asking it to play chess or solve one particular problem.

But the setup matters. A short conversation where a chatbot fools a few people is not sufficient. You want knowledgeable judges, enough time, and freedom to ask difficult follow-up questions. If a system can consistently hold up under that kind of examination, that’s strong evidence of human-level conversational intelligence. It doesn’t establish consciousness, and it doesn’t establish that the system is safe. Those are separate questions.

r001.rationale: The response describes the Turing test as a broad behavioral examination, but does not equate passing it with solving an AI-complete problem.

r002.rationale: The response says language can probe a broad range of abilities and allows difficult follow-ups, but does not clearly state that questions can come from any domain.

sol-6.1.text:
I favor the Turing test because it gives us a practical, behavioral standard. We don't have an agreed-upon definition of intelligence, and we can't directly inspect someone else's understanding. We infer it from what they can do and how they respond.

An unrestricted conversation can probe a very broad range of abilities: reasoning, humor, common sense, creativity, understanding context. If you can question a system at length, challenge it, follow up on its mistakes, and still can't distinguish it from a human, that's meaningful evidence of human-level performance.

It doesn't prove consciousness, and it doesn't establish that the system is safe. But as an operational test of human-like intelligence, it's a useful benchmark.
